title: The Constitutional Court of South Africa
hook: Born out of the end of apartheid, this court was designed to make a new constitution stick — and became one of the world's most-cited voices on what rights a government owes its people.
key_points: It is South Africa's highest court on constitutional matters, created as part of the post-apartheid constitutional settlement.
It can strike down laws and executive acts that conflict with the Constitution — judicial review of the strongest kind.
Its first landmark judgment struck down the death penalty as incompatible with the new Bill of Rights.
The Bill of Rights it enforces includes socio-economic rights — housing, health care, water — not just civil and political ones.
That makes it unusual: it has had to decide how far courts can go in reviewing what a government spends on basic needs.
content_html: When apartheid ended, South Africa faced a design question every new democracy faces in some form: how do you stop a future government from simply ignoring the constitution you just wrote? Its answer was a dedicated Constitutional Court, sitting at the top of the system for constitutional questions, with the authority to invalidate laws and government actions that clash with the new order.
extra_html:
The court is part of SCOTUSblog's series looking at high courts outside the United States, and it is a genuinely instructive comparison. Like many constitutional courts in the European tradition — and unlike the U.S. Supreme Court, which is a general appellate court that happens to decide constitutional cases — it was purpose-built for constitutional review. Its first landmark judgment struck down the death penalty as incompatible with the new Bill of Rights, an early signal that the court intended to give the document real force.

What has made it widely studied since is the content of the rights it enforces. South Africa's Bill of Rights reaches beyond the familiar civil and political liberties to include socio-economic guarantees such as housing, health care, and water. That confronts the court with a problem most constitutional courts can avoid: rights that cost money pull judges toward reviewing budget decisions, which elected branches normally own. How the court has tried to police those rights without simply taking over spending policy is a large part of why its reasoning gets cited well beyond South Africa.

related.title: The European Court of Justice
related.hook: A court above nations: it doesn't replace any country's supreme court, but it makes sure EU law means the same thing in every member state.

related.title: The Judiciary & Judicial Review
related.hook: Courts don't just settle disputes between people — through judicial review, many can also strike down a law or an official act that violates the constitution.

related.title: The Rule of Law
related.hook: The principle that everyone — including those in power — is bound by the same publicly known laws, applied equally.

related.title: What Human Rights Are
related.hook: Human rights are the radical claim that every person — regardless of country, status, or who's in charge — holds certain basic rights simply by being human.

flashcards.prompt: What is the Constitutional Court of South Africa's core role?
flashcards.back_html: It is the country's highest court on constitutional matters, with power to strike down laws and executive acts that conflict with the post-apartheid Constitution.

flashcards.prompt: What makes the Bill of Rights this court enforces unusual by global standards?

choices.text: It includes socio-economic rights like housing, health care, and water alongside civil and political rights
It applies only to citizens, not to residents or visitors
It can be amended by a simple majority of the cabinet

flashcards.explanation_html: Most bills of rights stop at civil and political liberties. South Africa's also commits the state to material basics, which the court then has to interpret.

flashcards.prompt: Why does enforcing socio-economic rights create a hard problem for a court?

choices.text: It pushes judges into reviewing how a government allocates its budget — normally a political choice
It requires the court to write new legislation itself
It means the court must approve every government contract

flashcards.explanation_html: Rights to housing or health care cost money, so enforcing them brushes against decisions elected branches usually make about spending priorities.
